newsitem.title: USA: Fiscal conservatives depressed by U.S. budget.
newsitem.headline: Fiscal conservatives depressed by U.S. budget.

text.p: When the Republican-majority Congress opened in 1995 it declared war on federal spending. Now that legislators are going home, fiscal conservatives say the budget revolution was just a skirmish.

Some House Republicans have been trumpeting that they saved taxpayers $53 billion over two years. But many analysts, including some who wished the budget-cutters well, say the real savings were a fraction of that.

"Virtually every inch of ground that was gained in 1995 through the drudgery of the budget battle has now been surrendered back to President Clinton this year," said Stephen Moore, a fiscal conservative and budget analyst at the Cato Institute, who says the outcome was a "disaster."

"For some of these programmes, spending has gone down in real terms. But overall, government is bigger than it was last year, and the year before," said Dan Mitchell of the conservative Heritage Foundation, who was less critical of Republicans but said he was disappointed in the results.

When Republicans restored money for several of his pet spending priorities, Clinton, late Monday, signed a huge spending bill that was passed by Congress to fund the government for the fiscal year that began Tuesday.

The president, who says he wants a balanced budget but has resisted many Republican cuts, convinced Congress at the last minute to spend $6 billion more than it had planned in fiscal 1997 in areas like education and street police.

The White House hailed its victory. "The Congress has in fact recognised that the American people support those priorities. That's why we were able to get this done," White House chief of staff Leon Panetta said.

But the Republicans also tried to win the public relations battle. Last month the House Appropriations Committee issued a news release saying: "Once we finish this year's appropriations process, Republicans will have saved American taxpayers $53 billion since taking control of Congress two years ago."

Elizabeth Morra, a spokeswoman for the committee, said Wednesday that number had been reached by estimating the cumulative amount of what would have been spent on non-defence, "discretionary" programmes had the Republicans not taken power away from Democrats on Capitol Hill.

Morro said that while the actual amount now budgeted for those programmes was $9 billion less than it had been when Republicans gained the majority, that figure did not tell the whole story of how much was saved.
"The $53 billion is money that would have been spent if we had stayed on the course we were on," she said -- an approach sometimes called "baseline" budgeting.

Budget analyst Stan Collender of the Burson-Marsteller public relations firm protested that baseline budgeting was just the kind of smoke-and-mirrors calculation the Republicans said they were going to stop.

"The only way they can claim that much savings is by using a baseline. If they compare everything to the prior year, they haven't saved virtually anything," Collender said. "Even $9 billion over two years is virtually insignificant compared to what they promised when they won control of Congress.
"They promised $900 billion in deficit reduction over seven years to balance the budget, and a tax cut," he said.
Many think the difference between the Republicans' arduous goal and their results was that they now face re-election and do not want to be accused of cutting things constituents want.
But Moore said Republican resolve had weakened much earlier, after Clinton began declaring it was their fault the government had shut down in budget battles last year.
"We're in the second year of the budget regime and already they have slipped," Moore said. "I don't have any confidence they will get back on track to balance the budget by 2002."
Collender is more optimistic. He thinks Clinton might be more interested in actively pursuing a balanced budget if he is re-elected -- partly with an eye on the history books.

"The deficit has gone down for four years straight under Clinton. If he's re-elected and gets the deficit going down for four more years, that will be the first time a president has either reduced the deficit or increased the surplus for eight years straight," Collender said.
